story867:
Before the world had shape, there was only Shipapu — a dark opening in the earth through which the first light would eventually shine. From within this darkness, the voice of Tsichtinako — Thought Woman — spoke. She could not be seen, for she was a spirit without a body, a voice without a face. But her words were precise as starlight.

"Two sisters must emerge," she said. "Iatiku — Life Bringer — and Nautsiti — Full Basket. They will carry the seeds of everything that lives."

The sisters climbed upward from the underworld, emerging into a world of blinding light and empty plains. Tsichtinako placed two baskets in their hands: one filled with seeds — corn, beans, squash, sunflower — and one filled with animal figurines of wood and stone, each one carved with the likeness of a creature that did not yet exist.

"Pray to the Sun, your father," Tsichtinako instructed. "He created this world from a clot of his own blood. Without his warmth, nothing will grow."

The sisters knelt and prayed. The Sun — Uchtsiti — looked down from the sky and sent his rays to warm the earth. Where his light touched the soil, it turned from gray to brown to rich, dark loam. The sisters planted the seeds from their baskets, and from the earth rose the mountains, the rivers, the plains.

Iatiku created the Corn Mother — a figure of power and abundance — and the Kachinas, spirits who would bring rain and fertility. Nautsiti, proud and independent, introduced death into the world when she disobeyed a taboo, walking where she was told not to walk and touching what she was told not to touch.

The sisters became the mothers of the Acoma people. Iatiku's children became the clans — the Corn Clan, the Sun Clan, the Kachina Clan — each one carrying a piece of the original gift. The story explains the origins of ceremonies, clans, and the relationship between the people, the land, and the spirits who watch from above.

The baskets that Tsichtinako gave are still represented in Acoma ceremonies, carried by priests who walk the paths the sisters first walked, planting hope in the dry earth.
story868:
In the beginning, the first people lived in darkness beneath the earth. They dwelt in four underground worlds, each one a layer of development, each one a step closer to the light they had never seen.

In the deepest world, they were barely human — small, blind, their hands and feet webbed, their bodies covered in slime. They could not speak or think. They were more dream than flesh.

But the spirits watched. Culture heroes and twin war gods came to them in the darkness and said, "Climb. There is a world above this one where the light is."

A giant reed grew from the floor of the underworld, pushing upward through layers of rock and soil. The people gathered at its base and began to climb. The reed was hollow, and the climb was long — through the third world, the second world, the first world — each time finding themselves still incomplete.

As they climbed, they changed. In the third world, they gained the ability to see — though the light was painful, and they covered their eyes. In the second world, they gained speech — though their first words were clumsy, like a child learning to walk. In the first world, they gained thought — though their thoughts were simple, like ripples on still water.

The last to emerge were an old man and an old woman who became trapped at the top of the reed. They could not make the final climb. "We will stay here," the old man said. "We will become the rulers of the dead. All who die must pass through our world before they can be reborn."

The sipapu — the opening through which they emerged — is sacred to all Pueblo peoples. It is identified with the Grand Canyon, or with a specific location within each Pueblo's traditional territory. It is the place where the living remember they came from darkness, and where the dead must return.
story870:
In Pueblo mythology, the Twin War Gods — Masewi and Oyoyewi — were born to a virgin mother who conceived from the rays of the Sun. They were not merely warriors but creators, beings whose power shaped the world itself.

When they were born, the earth shook. Their mother placed them on a blanket of eagle feathers, and they grew with supernatural speed — from infants to toddlers to young men in the space of a single day. They carried weapons made of lightning: arrows that could split mountains and shields that could stop the wind.

A great monster terrorized the Pueblo people. It was so large it could swallow an entire village in one bite — homes, people, cornfields, all disappearing into its gaping maw. The people tried to fight it with spears and arrows, but their weapons bounced off its hide like rain off a rock.

The Twin War Gods tracked the monster across the desert. They followed its trail of destruction — flattened hills, dried rivers, the bones of those it had consumed. When they found it, it was sleeping in a canyon, its body blocking the sun.

Masewi struck first, his lightning arrow piercing the monster's left eye. Oyoyewi followed, his arrow finding the right eye. The monster thrashed, but the twins were relentless. They shot arrow after arrow until the creature fell, its death creating a new valley where the people would later build their homes.

After their victory, the twins established the four directions, brought order to the world, and taught the people how to live — when to plant, when to harvest, when to dance and pray. When their work was done, they returned to the underworld, but they never left entirely. They watch from below, ready to return if the people need them again.
story871:
Kahp-too-óo-yoo — Corn-stalk Young Man — was the most powerful hunter, warrior, and wizard in Isleta. He could control the clouds. When he sang, rain fell. When he danced, thunder rolled. The people depended on him, and he never failed them.

But he had a friend who was not a friend. The false friend was jealous of Kahp-too-óo-yoo's power and devised a scheme. He invited the wizard to a ceremony, and during the night, he bewitched Kahp-too-óo-yoo and imprisoned him in the top of a giant pine tree that reached the sky.

The tree was enormous — its trunk as wide as a house, its branches lost in the clouds. Kahp-too-óo-yoo was trapped at the very top, where the wind never stopped and the cold never relented. He sang his rain songs, but the wind carried them away before they could reach the sky.

The village suffered. The clouds came but did not rain. The crops withered. The people grew thin. They did not know where Kahp-too-óo-yoo had gone.

But the Little Black Ant knew. She was small enough to climb any tree, and she found Kahp-too-óo-yoo sitting in the top of the great pine, his flute silent, his songs wasted.

The Little Black Ant went to the village and summoned the armies of the Little Black Ants and the Big Red Ants. Thousands of them marched to the base of the tree. They climbed in lines that covered the trunk like a living carpet.

At the top, the ants placed a cup of cornmeal and honey where Kahp-too-óo-yoo could reach it. Then, with the Black Ants pushing from above and the Red Ants pulling from below, they drove the giant pine tree deep into the earth.

The ground shook. The tree sank. And Kahp-too-óo-yoo walked free. He picked up his flute and played a song of rain. The clouds gathered. The rain fell. The crops revived.

He returned to the village playing his flute, and the people danced. The ants had saved them — the smallest creatures in the world, proving that no being is too small to make a difference.
story872:
Tsichtinako spoke from within the earth, a voice without a body, a mind without a face. The sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti could not see her, but they heard her as clearly as they heard the wind.

"Take the seeds from your baskets," Tsichtinako said, "and plant them in the earth. Each seed has a purpose. Corn will feed your children. Beans will climb the cornstalks and fix the soil. Squash will spread its leaves to shade the ground and keep the water from evaporating."

The sisters planted. They made prayer sticks — pahos — from reeds and feathers, and placed them at the four corners of their fields. Tsichtinako taught them how to arrange the prayers, how to face each direction, how to speak to the Sun Father and the Earth Mother.

"Name everything," Tsichtinako said. "The naming gives it power. Name the corn and it will grow. Name the rain and it will come. Name the directions — East, South, West, North — and the world will have order."

Iatiku named the plants. Nautsiti named the animals. Together they named the mountains and rivers, the clouds and winds, the stars and the shadows. Each name was a prayer, each prayer a thread connecting the people to the world.

Tsichtinako also taught them to organize their society into clans. The Corn Clan would tend the fields. The Kachina Clan would perform the ceremonies. The Arrow Clan would protect the village. Each clan had its duties, its responsibilities, its place in the web of relationships that held the community together.

Tsichtinako continues to guide the Acoma people invisibly. She is the power of thought itself — the ability to imagine a world that does not yet exist and bring it into being. She is the voice that speaks in the quiet moments, when a farmer looks at the sky and knows it will rain, or a mother holds her child and knows it will grow.

The Acoma people say: "Tsichtinako is always with us. We cannot see her, but we hear her in every thought that brings us closer to the truth."
story873:
Across the mesas and valleys of the Pueblo world, the Kachinas — Katsinam — move in procession through the plazas, their masks painted with the symbols of every living thing. They are the spirits of ancestors, of natural forces, of all things in the universe — rocks, stars, animals, plants.

They reside in the San Francisco Peaks, north of Flagstaff, Arizona, where the snow never fully melts and the pines stand like a cathedral. For six months each year — from winter solstice to July — they leave the peaks and come to the pueblos, bringing rain, fertility, and blessings.

Each Kachina has a specific identity, a mask with its own colors and design, songs that are sung only for it, and a role in the ceremonial calendar. Crow Mother brings rain and protects the children. The warrior Kachinas police behavior, appearing at dances with weapons drawn to discipline those who disrespect the ceremony. The clown Kachinas — the Koyemshi — expose human pretension through comedy, acting outlandish and foolish to remind people not to take themselves too seriously.

When a man wears the Kachina mask, he does not merely represent the spirit — he becomes it. The mask is not a costume but a face. The dancer's identity is subsumed. He speaks with the Kachina's voice. He moves with the Kachina's step. He sees the world through the Kachina's eyes.

The tihu — Kachina dolls — given to children are not toys. They are teaching objects, carved to help children recognize each Kachina and learn its songs and stories. A child who knows the Kachinas is a child who understands the world.

The Kachinas emerged from the underworld with the people. They were there in the beginning, in the darkness, in the climb. They are the oldest friends of the Pueblo people, and their return each winter is as certain as the turning of the earth.
story874:
Corn was not always there. Before the Holy People gave it, the people survived on roots and berries, on whatever the earth offered without being asked. They were hungry, always hungry.

In one tradition, the Corn Maidens brought corn to the people. Blue Corn Maiden was the most beautiful — her body the color of the evening sky, her hair the color of twilight. Yellow Corn Maiden followed, bright as the sun. White Corn Maiden came after, pale as dawn. Red Corn Maiden blushed like sunset. Black Corn Maiden carried the darkness of the deepest earth. And Speckled Corn Maiden, who was different from the others, carried the promise that difference was not deficiency.

They walked among the people, and where their feet touched the ground, corn grew. They taught the women how to grind the kernels into meal, how to make piki bread thin as paper and sweet as honeydew, how to store corn for winter so it would last through the lean months.

In another tradition, a boy discovered corn growing in a hidden place — a cave in the mountains, or a clearing in the forest where the Holy People had planted it. He brought the seeds to his village, and the people planted them in hills, three seeds to a hill, just as the Holy People had instructed.

The different colors of corn each have spiritual significance. White corn belongs to the East and dawn. Yellow to the West and twilight. Blue to the South and midday. Red to the fire. Black to the North and night. Speckled to the center, where all directions meet.

Corn is not merely food. It is a sentient being with which humans have a reciprocal relationship. Humans care for corn — planting, weeding, harvesting — and corn nourishes humans. This reciprocity is reflected in the ceremonies that accompany every stage of corn's life, from the first seed placed in the ground to the last ear stored in the granary.

The successful growth of corn depends not only on farming skill but on the proper performance of ceremonies and the people's moral conduct. A community that fights and lies will find its corn withering. A community that lives in harmony will find its fields heavy with ears.
